title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6:36–40)
hook: Gideon asks twice for a sign, and receives it

segments.voice: Yesterday, mighty: the angel's name for Gideon while he was still hiding in a winepress. Your line was a coat held out first. Today, the same man, still not sure.

Gideon lays a piece of wool, a fleece, on the threshing floor. Around him, everything is moving. The armies of Midian have crossed over and camped in the valley of Jezreel. Gideon has blown the shofar, and men from several tribes are gathering behind him. He has already been told he'll save Israel. He has already seen fire leap from a rock to take his offering. And still he wants one more sign, and he asks for it to come down with the dew.
screen: `THE ARMIES GATHER.` → `A FLEECE ON THE THRESHING FLOOR.` → `ONE MORE SIGN.`

segments.voice: If there's dew on the fleece only, he says, and the ground around it is dry, then I'll know you will save Israel by my hand, as you said. In the morning he gets up early and wrings out a bowl full of water. The ground is dry. That should be enough. It isn't. So he asks again, and listen to how: "Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once." This time, reverse it: a dry fleece, and dew on all the ground. And that night, the text says, God did so. Dry wool, wet earth. What the story leaves out is any anger. No rebuke, no lecture on faith. The sign is given, and given again, without a word of complaint. That matters, because the Torah also says not to put the Lord to the test. So readers argue over Gideon. Some say he was wrong to ask. Some say he wasn't asking about God at all, but about himself: was he really the one? The story doesn't settle it. It keeps the record: a frightened man doubted, said so out loud, politely, twice, and was answered both times.
screen: `DEW ON THE FLEECE, THE GROUND DRY.` · `LET NOT THINE ANGER BE HOT.` · `DRY FLEECE, WET GROUND.` · `NO REBUKE, BOTH TIMES.`

segments.voice: Let one honest doubt come up, about a decision, about yourself, or about God if that's where it lives, and name it plainly, the way Gideon did, without arguing it away or scolding it. Breathe with it beside you, as if it's allowed in the room. If you pray, bring it with his opening words: let not thine anger be hot against me.
Gideon's fleece. Wet when the ground was dry, then dry when the ground was wet: a doubter's sign, asked for twice and given twice.
Your line: doubt is allowed. Asking twice didn't make him less chosen. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read the fleece story in Judges 6 as part of the Former Prophets, and commentators debate whether Gideon's request was a forbidden test of God or a plea for reassurance.

chat.says: Isn't asking God for a sign kind of faithless? Did Gideon get in trouble for it?
options: No rebuke at all: he asked politely, twice, and was answered both times, though readers still argue.
Yes, God refused the second sign, because asking twice showed he had no faith at all.
He only asked once; the second sign came on its own, without him asking for it.
chat.meaning: The text records no anger: the sign is given twice. Because the Torah says not to test God, readers still argue whether he should have asked.

notes: Audit: hook no longer says Midian 'crossed the Jordan' (6:33 says only that they passed over and camped in the valley of Jezreel). Older notes about 'readers have argued for a long time' and dew 'settling on everything alike' refer to lines no longer in the script.
Judges 6:39 is quoted from the KJV because the JPS 1917 wording of this verse was not certain; a Keeper may swap in JPS.

'Readers have argued over Gideon for a long time' is general; the two readings (a forbidden test vs. a request about himself) are offered without naming commentators. A Keeper may wish to name specific ones.
'Men from several tribes' paraphrases 6:35 (Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, Naphtali); no count given in the script.
Dew 'settles on everything alike' is a plain observation used to frame the hook, not a claim from the text.
